« Je ne regrette rien, c’est le destin »: “I don’t regret anything, it’s destiny,” he says candidly.
Quelques jours après le triste anniversa: A few days after the sad anniversary of the Quebec City shooting, which took the lives of six men, we wanted to give Muslim men a chance to speak, in all humanity. They opened up despite their discomfort, their modesty – and their wish to stay strong and positive, which in itself is not surprising. Even so, as their words flow more freely, a deep weariness comes through. Here are their stories.
Aymen Derbali aurait pu être la septième: Aymen Derbali could have been the seventh victim of the attack on the Grand Mosque of Quebec City. He was hit by seven bullets. “The pain never ends. I have become the pain, in my back, in my hands, it’s electric fields all the time. I suffer every moment,” he confides in his living room. Despite his suffering, Aymen invited us into his home, opening his door wide. He smiles, can’t help joking, and offers us cookies. He doesn’t regret going to prayer on January 29, 2017, at the Islamic Cultural Centre of Quebec. “I don’t regret anything, it’s destiny,” he says candidly. On the night of the attack, he was setting up a new television for his son. “I looked at my watch, it was 7:25 p.m. If I had taken 5 more minutes, I wouldn’t have made it on time, because prayer starts at 7:30 p.m.” He considered praying at home before changing his mind. “I told myself: ‘No, I’m going to the mosque.’ I told my wife: ‘I’m going to say my prayer at the mosque and I’ll be back, I’ll finish setting up the TV afterward.’” Aymen never came back. In 100 seconds, the killer left 6 dead, 8 wounded and 17 orphans. “He was aiming for the heads. Most of them were shot in the head,” says Aymen. “The bullet I took in my hand, it was when I said the shahada (the prayer spoken by a dying person, who raises the index finger as a reminder of the oneness of God). As soon as I raised my hand, he aimed at my hand. He was trained, he wasn’t backing down. He had 50 bullets, he fired 48 of them in 100 seconds,” he recalls.
Le soir de l’attentat, un dimanche soir,: On the night of the attack, a Sunday night, there was only one woman at the mosque. A few children were in the basement for Quran classes. “On Sunday nights, it’s mostly men at the mosque,” explains Aymen Derbali. You have to understand that Jummah, the holy day of the week for Muslims, is Friday. That is when the most families are at the mosque. The killer had scouted the place before carrying out his massacre. He had already shown up at the mosque on a Friday to give alms, and on other occasions in the preceding weeks. Was he targeting Muslim men? Hard to know. Only one person – the killer – knows the answer. “He didn’t choose the time when there are the most women, he chose the time when there are the most men,” Aymen says. At the mosque, men and women are always separated. At the Islamic Cultural Centre of Quebec, the women’s prayer hall is upstairs. The killer stayed on the ground floor; he didn’t fire upward and didn’t go up to the second floor. “Maybe he preferred to kill men, I don’t know. But it’s obvious that Sunday night is when there are the most men.”
Le 29 janvier 2017, ce sont des familles: On January 29, 2017, entire families were affected by the attack. While men were targeted that night, Muslim women remain the main victims of Islamophobic acts in Quebec, because of the intersectionality of the issues they face. “Racism remains gendered, meaning there is an intersection of race and gender, which creates distinctions rather than competition,” explains Leïla Benhadjoudja, an expert in the sociology of racism and an assistant professor at the Institute of Feminist and Gender Studies at the University of Ottawa. She says, however, that the image of the barbaric, violent Muslim man is more insidious than people think. All the more so because very little academic research has looked into the subject. “As Edward Said reminds us, Islam is a trauma for Europe. After all, there was a Muslim civilization in Europe for several centuries… September 11, 2001 only accentuated this image, which associates Muslim men’s bodies with fear,” she points out. “In the collective imagination, their masculinity is dangerous and they are incapable of tenderness or gentleness.” The Muslim man is thus seen as dangerous to the West, but also to Muslim women. In this context, the Quebec City attack somehow offered a rare opportunity to humanize Muslim men. “For once, we saw in the media a Muslim man – the victim Azzedine Soufiane, in particular – smiling and honoured for his kindness and bravery. Do we have to get to a massacre before we talk about them differently?”
Aymen Derbali dénonce <l1>le reportage e: Aymen Derbali denounces <l1>the erroneous TVA Nouvelles report</l1>, broadcast 11 months after the attack, which claimed that a Montréal mosque had asked for women to be excluded from a neighbouring construction site on prayer day. “Some media outlets try to provoke us to get the public to think that we don’t accept the norm, that we want to make our own laws,” he says. He cites as an example the narrative presenting the Muslim man as someone who doesn’t let women work, a stereotype that is far from reality. He points to the role the media play in spreading these representations. “Unfortunately, it’s often journalists who convey the cliché of the macho Muslim man who belittles women and considers that they have no rights, when that is totally false,” he says. Media coverage of wars in Muslim-majority countries feeds fear. “There are attacks, and the media spread the cliché of the hard, violent Muslim man who is scary,” laments the father of the family.
Ce cliché, Aymen Derbali l’a subi dans s: Aymen Derbali has lived with this cliché in his professional life. At times, he has felt that he couldn’t live his Muslim identity normally. In 2005, he took an English immersion course at Bishop’s University. He wore a long beard at the time. A discussion about immigration came up in a course on multiculturalism. A Quebecer student claimed that immigrants come to Canada because their countries are poor, and Aymen corrected her, telling her that this claim was unfounded. The student replied by asking him why he didn’t go back to his own country. “I got angry and said: ‘Mind your business!’” he remembers. A few days later, a classmate warned him: “Be careful, she said she was afraid you’d plant a bomb at the university.” For Aymen, this experience clearly shows the prejudice that an upset Muslim man is a potential terrorist. “There are people who think that if a Muslim gets angry, he’s going to plant a bomb, he’s going to commit an act of terrorism. He’s a human being like everyone else, who yells and gets angry too!” he exclaims. It is this kind of cliché that, in his view, contributed to the Quebec City attack. Aymen Derbali was an information technology consultant. He worked for large companies and for certain provincial and municipal bodies. In 2014, he was working at a government agency when the <l1>shooting on Parliament Hill</l1> took place. The next day, the head of his internal department started ignoring him. “She wouldn’t answer when I said hello. A month later, the director asked for me to be replaced and transferred to another department. I asked for the reasons, and no one gave me any.”
« C’est rare qu’on a la chance de se vid: “It’s rare that we get the chance to get things off our chest. Muslim women suffer a lot, and it’s normal to offer them a listening ear and platforms. But men struggle too, and often in silence,” ventures Munir hesitantly; he arrived from Pakistan nearly 20 years ago. Of course, racism and Islamophobia didn’t begin on January 29, 2017. Where many Muslim men feel it most is in the job market. If violence in the workplace comes up often in conversations, it’s because that is where they most often feel vulnerable. That is where their pride and honour are hit. “The rest of the time, we manage to ignore it, to live with it. But when you have to feed your family, the stakes change. You feel trapped, you’re suffocating,” illustrates Munir, who works in the restaurant industry. For him, the feeling of powerlessness is the worst. “Most of the time, I find myself in situations where I can’t say anything so I don’t lose my job. I always have to smile and play it down. It gets heavy.” Jamal now refuses to put on fake smiles. He no longer censors himself in debates either, at the risk of “coming across as aggressive.” “How do I deal with Islamophobia and racism? It’s going to sound intense, but I’ve made the choice to stop working for Quebec employers,” says Jamal right off the bat; he is an engineer and father who has lived in Montréal for more than 10 years. It is, in a way, his means of countering the powerlessness Munir describes.
S’il en est arrivé à ce choix radical, c: He reached this radical choice because microaggressions, especially in the job market, pushed him to the breaking point. He remembers his early days in particular. Despite solid experience in his field, the hundreds of résumés he sent out went nowhere. One day, he ran into a childhood friend from Morocco, who works for the company he was trying to get into and for which he is perfectly qualified. The company that is still advertising positions but never calls him back, despite his many calls. “He admitted to me that the secretary had a very particular strategy for screening résumés: she simply set aside the ones whose names she couldn’t pronounce easily.” Since that day, Jamal has changed his compound surname to simplify it. Over time, the engineer gained enough experience that he no longer has to send out résumés. In fact, the opposite now happens: he is sought after for his expertise. He now has options. “Since I’ve had the choice, I no longer work for employers from here. I live in Quebec, but my clients are in Ontario and the United States. And, yes, I feel a difference when it comes to racism,” he says bluntly.

Mais les changements se font-ils trop le: But is change happening too slowly? Aymen thinks so. “We don’t speak out loudly enough. There are incidents, and the police step in more than before, sometimes. But people don’t understand the limit, or the difference, between freedom of expression and hate speech,” he believes. He wants far-right groups to be listed and prosecuted as terrorist organizations. Five years later, Aymen still lives in Quebec City. Several of the survivors and those who escaped from the Muslim community of Sainte-Foy have left the national capital for Ontario. Aymen now wants us to examine the reasons for and consequences of the January 29 attack. “If there is no political will on the part of the provincial government, all the efforts we can make to fight Islamophobia won’t have much impact,” says the survivor. He feels he must take action for the six men, six brothers, who fell beside him five years ago. “My blood mixed with theirs on the carpet. I have a duty to honour their memory: to fight, to get involved in the fight against Islamophobia and all forms of discrimination – whether against Black people, against Indigenous people, against any community that suffers from it. Because they fell because of Islamophobia. As long as we don’t fight effectively, the danger is there. It will always be lying in wait for us.”
